claims.text: Reducing heating and cooling rates will increase the time available for atomic diffusion in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Enhanced atomic diffusion will mitigate kinetic trapping during nanoparticle synthesis.
Mitigating kinetic trapping will promote a more uniform single-phase solid solution.
Reducing heating and cooling rates will improve elemental homogeneity.
Reducing heating and cooling rates will produce more controlled particle morphology.
Nanoparticles made under the baseline rapid thermal processing exhibit phase separation.
Nanoparticles made under the baseline rapid thermal processing exhibit elemental segregation.
Nanoparticles made under the baseline rapid thermal processing exhibit irregular or uncontrolled morphology.
Atomic diffusion kinetics govern atomic mixing and phase homogenization in this synthesis regime.
Rapid thermal processing limits the time available for atomic diffusion.
Limited diffusion causes kinetic trapping of metastable, nonequilibrium configurations.
Kinetically trapped configurations cause phase separation and elemental segregation.
Slower thermal ramps allow the nanoparticles to approach thermodynamic equilibrium.
Approaching thermodynamic equilibrium stabilizes a single-phase solid solution in the applicable compositions.
The proposed mechanism applies particularly to noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements under rapid, nonequilibrium thermal processing.
The mechanism may not apply under near-equilibrium or extremely slow processing when diffusion is not kinetically limiting.
The magnitude of improvement may depend on the synthesis parameters and elemental composition.
